name: Prim's Minimum Spanning Tree
tagline: Growing a minimum-weight cycle-free spanning tree from a root vertex in $O((V + E) \log V)$ using the Cut Property and a min-heap.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of Prim's algorithm—from the Cut Property proof to lazy-deletion binary heaps, $O(V^2)$ dense-graph arrays, and avoiding visited-on-push bugs.

spark.summary: Prim's algorithm grows a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) from a single start vertex by repeatedly picking the lowest-weight edge that connects a visited vertex to an unvisited vertex using a min-heap.
spark.keyTakeaway: Prim's excels on dense graphs and incremental frontier expansion in $O((V + E) \log V)$ time with a binary heap—no global edge sort or Union-Find structure required.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Given a connected, undirected, weighted graph $G = (V, E)$, a **Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)** is a subset of $V - 1$ edges connecting all vertices with no cycles and minimum total edge weight.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Prim's Greedy Frontier Growth on Graph {A,B,C,D,E} (Root A (w=0) -> B (edge A-B=2) -> C (edge B-C=1) -> D->E (4 + 2)); Prim's MST Execution & Connectivity Verification (Graph Builder -> Min-Heap / Array -> MST Set S).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Graph density $E / V^2$ determines which MST data structure runs fastest in practice. A network planning tool computes the minimum-cost fiber backbone across $V = 250$ regional PoPs ($E \approx 18,000$ candidate dark-fiber links) using Prim's $O(V^2)$ array scan in.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Compare Prim's with Kruskal's MST, shortest-path algorithms, and heap priority queues.

learningJourney.title: What is Prim's Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithm
learningJourney.explanation:
Given a connected, undirected, weighted graph $G = (V, E)$, a **Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)** is a subset of $V - 1$ edges connecting all vertices with no cycles and minimum total edge weight. **Prim's algorithm** grows the MST greedily from a root vertex: at each step, it selects the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut between visited vertices $S$ and unvisited vertices $V \setminus S$.

Its correctness follows directly from the **Cut Property**: the lightest edge crossing any cut $(S, V \setminus S)$ must belong to an MST.

sectionDiagram.title: Prim's Greedy Frontier Growth on Graph {A,B,C,D,E}

cards.label: 1. Seed Root
cards.detail: Mark A visited; push (2, B) and (3, C) onto the min-heap.

cards.label: 2. Pop Minimum
cards.detail: Pop (2, B), mark B visited on pop, and push (1, C) and (4, D).

cards.label: 3. Skip Stale
cards.detail: Later when stale (3, C) pops, C is already in visited so it is skipped.

sectionDiagram.summary: Unlike Dijkstra's (which pushes dist[u] + w), Prim's pushes only the single crossing edge weight w(u, v).

learningJourney.title: Why we need Prim's (and why Visited-on-Push breaks it)
learningJourney.explanation: Connecting $V$ data centers, substations, or sensors with minimum total cable cost and zero cycles requires an MST. When implementing Prim's with a binary min-heap (`heapq` / `PriorityQueue`), the #1 bug is marking `visited[v] = True` when *pushing* `(w, v)` instead of when *popping*—which locks in the first-seen edge rather than the minimum-weight edge.

ideas.title: Handles Negative Edge Weights Natively
ideas.description: Because Prim's compares single edge weights across a cut rather than cumulative path sums, negative edge weights work without modification (unlike Dijkstra's).

ideas.title: MST Is Not a Shortest-Path Tree
ideas.description: An MST minimizes the *sum of all edge weights* across the network; individual node pairs may take more hops than their Dijkstra shortest path.

learningJourney.title: Where Prim's excels (and where Kruskal's or Edmonds' fit)
learningJourney.explanation: Choose Prim's on dense graphs or adjacency-list frontier expansions; switch to Kruskal's on sparse edge lists or Edmonds' on directed graphs.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Dense Graphs ($E \approx V^2$) & Adjacency Lists
benefits: $O(V^2)$ array-scan Prim's beats $O(E \log E)$ Kruskal's on complete graphs with zero heap or Union-Find memory.
costs: Must verify `len(visited) == V` at the end if the input graph may be disconnected.

benefits: Kruskal's with path-compressed Union-Find often has better cache locality on flat edge arrays.
costs: Kruskal's requires sorting all $E$ edges upfront.

benefits: Use Chu-Liu/Edmonds' algorithm for Minimum Spanning Arborescence on directed graphs.
costs: Prim's requires symmetric undirected edges (`u->v` and `v->u`).

learningJourney.title: How Lazy-Deletion Prim's is implemented cleanly
learningJourney.explanation: Use lazy deletion with a standard binary min-heap (`heapq`): push `(edge_w, neighbor)` without decrease-key bookkeeping, check `if u in visited: continue` immediately after `heappop`, and assert `len(visited) == n` to catch disconnected components.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Binary Heap vs. $O(V^2)$ Array vs. Kruskal's
learningJourney.explanation: Graph density $E / V^2$ determines which MST data structure runs fastest in practice.

benefits: $O((V + E) \log V)$ time, 15 lines of code, no decrease-key pointer management.
costs: Heap can hold up to $O(E)$ stale entries on very dense graphs.

benefits: $O(V^2)$ time and zero heap overhead—fastest when $E > V^2 / \log V$.
costs: Quadratic $O(V^2)$ time and matrix space on sparse graphs.

benefits: $O(E \log E)$ time; naturally produces a spanning forest on disconnected graphs.
costs: Slower than $O(V^2)$ Prim's on dense graphs due to sorting $V^2$ edges.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a binary-heap implementation of Prim's algorithm, what happens if you mark a neighbor `v` as `visited` when *pushing* `(w, v)` to the heap rather than when *popping* it?

options.text: You lock in the first-discovered edge to `v` instead of the minimum-weight edge, potentially producing a non-minimal spanning tree
options.feedback: Correct: only mark `visited` when popping from the min-heap so lighter edges discovered later can still win.

options.text: The algorithm enters an infinite loop
options.feedback: It terminates, but with a suboptimal total weight.

options.text: It converts Prim's algorithm into Kruskal's algorithm
options.feedback: Kruskal's sorts edges globally and uses Union-Find.
